```
Manage workspaces

Usage:
  spin workspace [flags]
  spin workspace [command]

Aliases:
  workspace, ws

Available Commands:
  console     What the workspace's machine printed to its serial console
  create      Create a new workspace
  delete      Delete a workspace
  egress      What a workspace has reached beyond this installation
  get         Get workspace details
  history     Show workspace state change history
  list        List your workspaces
  logs        Search what the workspace's machine printed to its console
  policies    The network policies a workspace can be created with
  recover     Re-home a workspace whose host is gone
  reset       Put a stopped workspace's disk back to what it was created from
  restore     Put a stopped workspace's disk back to a snapshot, or to what it was created from
  retag       Change which network policies a workspace runs under
  start       Start a stopped workspace
  status      Why a workspace is not behaving
  stop        Stop a running workspace
  suspend     Put a running workspace down with its processes where they are
  update      Update workspace properties

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for workspace

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")

Use "spin workspace [command] --help" for more information about a command.
```

### spin workspace console

```
Show the tail of a workspace's serial console: the kernel, then the guest's init,
then the supervisor.

This is where a machine that never came up says why. It is read from the host that holds
it, so a workspace that has moved to another host has nothing here about the run that failed
on the one it left - unless the installation collects consoles, and then 'spin workspace logs'
searches what every run of it printed.

Usage:
  spin workspace console <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help          help for console
      --lines int32   How many lines from the end (default 200)

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace create

```
Create a new workspace from an image or a snapshot. An image is a published starting disk
the installation allows; without --image, the installation's default is used. Resources left
unset take the installation's defaults.

Examples:
  spin workspace create --name mydev
  spin workspace create --name mydev --cpu 2 --memory 4096
  spin workspace create --name build --env GOPROXY=direct --network-tag registry-only
  spin workspace create --name copy --from-snapshot <snapshot-id>

Usage:
  spin workspace create [flags]

Flags:
      --cpu int32              CPU cores (default: the installation's)
      --disk int32             Free disk space in GB (default: the installation's)
      --env strings            Environment variables (KEY=VALUE)
      --from-snapshot string   Start from a snapshot instead of an image
  -h, --help                   help for create
      --image string           the ref of the disk image to start from, with its version (default: the base image of the machine this installation runs)
      --memory int32           Memory in MB (default: the installation's)
      --name string            Workspace name (auto-generated if empty)
      --network-tag strings    Network policy to run under, by name (repeatable)
      --port int32             Port to expose
      --team string            Team ID (personal workspace if empty)
      --timeout duration       How long --wait waits (default 5m0s)
      --wait                   Return once the workspace is running

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace egress

```
List every destination a running workspace's machine has been allowed to reach, with the
host's own packet and byte counters and, where its resolver answered for it, the name it was
asked for.

This is what an allowlist is written from: a network policy is a list of destinations, and a
guess at one either breaks the workspace or allows what nobody meant to. The host keeps the
record for six hours, so a workspace has to be running on one to answer.

Usage:
  spin workspace egress <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for egress

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace logs

```
Search the workspace's console as the installation kept it, newest first: every run
of it, on whichever host ran it, for the installation's retention.

Only where the installation collects consoles (collect_workspace_logs); otherwise
'spin workspace console' reads the tail from the host that holds it.

Examples:
  spin workspace logs my-ws
  spin workspace logs my-ws 'panic OR "out of memory"' --since 24h

Usage:
  spin workspace logs <workspace> [query] [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help             help for logs
      --limit int32      how many lines, newest first: 1 to 1000 (default 100)
      --since duration   how far back to look, at most 744h (31 days) (default 1h0m0s)

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace policies

```
List the network policies the hosts report they enforce, by name: these are the words
'spin workspace create --network-tag' takes.

A policy is an installation's, not a workspace's: an operator writes it on each host, and the
host is what enforces it. A tag no host reports is refused at create rather than failing when
the workspace starts. Where two hosts give one name different prefixes, both are shown: a tag
that means two things is a misconfiguration worth seeing.

Usage:
  spin workspace policies [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for policies

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace recover

```
Move a workspace to another host after the one it was on died.

A workspace cannot be started on a host that is not connected, and no amount of retrying
changes that. Recovering takes its disk from the dead host and places it on a live one.

The cost is the work the dead host had written and not yet published. Run without
--accept-data-loss to see that cost; nothing is changed until you pass it.

Usage:
  spin workspace recover <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
      --accept-data-loss   go ahead and give up the work the old host had not published
  -h, --help               help for recover

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace reset

```
Put a stopped workspace's disk back to the snapshot it was created from: the image, or
the snapshot it was made from. Everything the workspace has ever written is given up.

Nothing is uploaded and nothing is downloaded - the disk it goes back to is one its host
already has - so this is the cheapest way back there is. The disk it had is kept with its
snapshots, so a snapshot taken before the reset is still a way back to that work.

Usage:
  spin workspace reset <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help               help for reset
      --start              Start the workspace on the disk it was created from and wait until it is running
      --timeout duration   How long --start waits (default 5m0s)
  -y, --yes                Skip confirmation

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace restore

```
Put a stopped workspace's disk back to one of its snapshots. Without a snapshot, the
disk goes back to what the workspace was created from.

Everything the workspace wrote after the snapshot is given up, which is why the workspace has
to be stopped first. The disk it had is kept with its snapshots, so restoring to a snapshot
taken after the one restored undoes the restore.

With --with-memory the snapshot's running processes come back too, from the instant it was
taken, and the workspace may be running: it is put back to that instant.

Usage:
  spin workspace restore <workspace> [snapshot-id] [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help               help for restore
      --start              Start the workspace on the restored disk and wait until it is running
      --timeout duration   How long --start waits (default 5m0s)
      --with-memory        Resume the snapshot's processes too; the workspace may be running

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace retag

```
Replace the network policies a workspace runs under, while it runs. The host is told
at once, so a change takes effect without a restart.

The tags given are the whole set, not an addition: 'retag ws --network-tag web' leaves the
workspace carrying web and nothing else. Naming none means what it means on a create - the
installation's default. To have a workspace reach nothing, name the policy 'offline', which
every host has.

Taking a policy away closes what it opened, including the connections the workspace already
had: the addresses its lookups opened under the leaving policies are forgotten and its open
connections are dropped, so the next packet of each is judged by the policy as it now is.
Adding a policy closes nothing.

You may choose among the policies the installation declares ('spin workspace policies'). An
administrator may name any policy a host reports.

Usage:
  spin workspace retag <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help                  help for retag
      --network-tag strings   Network policy to run under, by name (repeatable); the whole set, not an addition

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace status

```
Show what each party believes about a workspace, and where they disagree.

A workspace's state is held by four parties that can disagree: the control plane has a
lifecycle state it set, the supervisor inside the guest reports what it is doing, the host
either heartbeats or does not, and the volume either serves the disk or refuses. "spin workspace get" shows the first of those. This shows all four, and names the
gaps between them - which is usually the answer.

Usage:
  spin workspace status <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for status

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```

### spin workspace suspend

```
Checkpoint a running workspace's memory and disk and stop its machine. Its next start
resumes that instant - the processes go on from where they were, on any host carrying the same
machine, not only the one it was suspended on.

This is what a host being drained does to what it runs. It answers once the memory is stored
and the disk is published, which takes as long as that does; the machine runs until then, and
what it does in that window is given up.

The checkpoint is a snapshot like any other: 'spin snapshot list' shows it, and deleting it is
what makes the workspace start from its disk instead.

Usage:
  spin workspace suspend <workspace> [flags]

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for suspend

Global Flags:
      --config string    config file (default is $HOME/.spin/config.yaml)
  -o, --output string    text for a person, or json: one document of what the API answered, and no prose (default "text")
      --profile string   named profile to use (default "default")
```
